t.1.167.1: Then the sage, seeing his hermitage bereft of those sons, went forth once again from that hermitage, stricken with deep grief.
t.1.167.2: He saw a river, O Pārtha, swollen with new water in the rainy season, carrying along many trees of various kinds that had grown upon its banks.
t.1.167.4: Then the great sage, deeply grief-stricken, bound himself tightly with fetters and plunged into the waters of that great river.
t.1.167.3: Then, O delight of the Pauravas, filled with sorrow, he again fell to brooding: “Let me drown myself in her waters.”
t.1.167.6: Then, freed from his fetters, that great seer climbed out of the water, and the great seer gave this river the name Vipāśā.
t.1.167.5: Then, O crusher of enemy forces, the river cut his bonds, set the seer on level ground, and released him freed of his fetters.
t.1.167.7: Then he set his mind upon grief and did not remain in one place; he went to the mountains, to the rivers, and to the lakes.
t.1.167.8: Then the sage, once again, seeing a river flowing from the Himālaya and teeming with fierce crocodiles, threw himself down into its current.
t.1.167.9: That best of rivers, regarding the brahmin as equal to fire, fled away in a hundred directions; because of this she is renowned as the Śatadru.
t.1.167.10: Then, seeing himself by himself come to dry land there too, he said, "It is not possible to die," and went back again to the hermitage.
t.1.167.12: "Who is this that follows me?" he said. His daughter-in-law answered him: "I am Adṛśyantī by name, O greatly fortunate one, the wife of Śakti, an ascetic woman devoted to austerity."
t.1.167.11: As he walked toward his hermitage, followed by his daughter-in-law Adṛśyantī, he happened to hear behind him the sound of Vedic recitation, adorned with the six Aṅgas complete in their meaning.
t.1.167.13: Daughter, whose is this sound of recitation of the Veda with its Aṅgas? It is like the recitation of the Veda with its Aṅgas that I once heard from Śakti.
t.1.167.15: Thus addressed, the seer Vasiṣṭha, partaker of the highest, rejoiced, and saying, "There is an offspring," he turned back from death, Pārtha.
t.1.167.14: This child in my womb is the offspring of Śakti, your son. For twelve years he has been here, reciting the Vedas, O sage.
t.1.167.16: Then, O sinless one, as he was returning together with that daughter-in-law, he saw Kalmāṣapāda seated in the lonely forest.
t.1.167.18: But Adṛśyantī, seeing that doer of cruel deeds before her, spoke these words to Vasiṣṭha in a voice trembling with fear.
t.1.167.17: But as soon as the king saw him, O Bhārata, he rose up in anger, and, possessed by the fierce rakṣas, he then sought to devour him.
t.1.167.19: O blessed one, yonder a terrible Rākṣasa is coming this way like Death with his fierce rod, a club of wood held firmly in his grasp.
t.1.167.20: There is no one else on earth today who is able to restrain him except you, O greatly fortunate one, best among all who know the Vedas.
t.1.167.21: Save me, blessed lord, from this evil one of dreadful appearance! Surely this Rākṣasa means to do this: to devour the two of us here.
